title: A network with no discoverable center: the cult of Mithras across the Roman frontier
register: archaeological, and skeptical of the network it names
summary: Small congregations met in narrow, cave-like rooms from Ostia to a fort on the Euphrates, sharing one god, one bull-killing image, and a common grammar of grades and communal meals — carried less by any organization than by the roads, rivers, and postings that moved soldiers, customs officers, and traders who happened to belong. No founder, headquarters, correspondence, or treasury is known to have held the cells together; what repeats across the empire is the iconography and the ritual vocabulary, not a chain of command. It did not end in a single stroke: imperial law made its sacrifices a crime in 391–392, and individual rooms were abandoned, filled, converted, or simply fell silent on their own local timetables through the decades after.

nodes.name: Rome
nodes.note: The largest known concentration of cells, and probably an early center for the iconographic package that spread from it, with sculptors' workshops to match. Also the setting of a late-fourth-century senatorial circle that included men who held the title pater patrum. An often-cited estimate of roughly 680–700 possible congregations in the city is an extrapolation from population and building capacity, not an archaeological count; only a small number of buildings survives. The imperial laws of 391–392 that made open sacrifice a crime were issued for an empire that still had Rome at its notional center.

nodes.name: Rome, Santa Prisca
nodes.note: A converted basement sanctuary with paintings, ritual texts, benches, and a cult niche, in use by about 200 CE and dated partly by a graffito of 202. Older claims that Christians violently destroyed it around 400 have been reassessed: the damage is real, but some of it may be structural decay or even modern excavation and restoration harm — illustrated by a head of Mithras reportedly lost in a 1953 restoration, not in antiquity.

nodes.name: Ostia
nodes.note: Rome's port, and the clearest urban laboratory for the network: at least sixteen to eighteen structures classified as Mithraic or closely related, scattered through houses, warehouses, baths, and the imperial palace rather than gathered in one sacred quarter. Its mix of port officials, freedmen, slaves, traders, and craftsmen weighs against a purely military account of the network; one tabulation found the military behind only 11 of 252 readable Italian inscriptions, a measure of what survives to be read rather than of total membership.

nodes.name: Ostia, Baths of Mithras sanctuary
nodes.note: A sanctuary about 15.37 by 4.55 meters, sunk into the service zone beneath a bathing complex and lit by two skylights; its marble tauroctony carries the Greek signature of the sculptor Kriton the Athenian. Pieces of the cult statue were later found deposited in a drain, and a Christian oratory was built above the sanctuary — a real sequence, though who broke the statue, and why, is not securely established.

nodes.name: Ostia, Felicissimus Mithraeum
nodes.note: Named for its donor Felicissimus, established in the second half of the third century. Its own closure is not independently dated in the surviving record.

nodes.name: Carnuntum
nodes.note: A legionary fortress, canabae, civil town, river crossing, and administrative hub on the middle Danube. An early dedication is associated with the centurion C. Sacidius Barbarus, dated mainly by inference from the departure of Legio XV Apollinaris for the East under Trajan rather than by a fixed year on the stone. The large three-aisled Mithraeum III, excavated in 1894, and the 308 CE inscription in which the Tetrarchs restored a sanctuary and called Mithras fautor imperii sui make Carnuntum the clearest case of imperial-level patronage of one specific site, not proof of an empire-wide Mithraic state cult.

nodes.name: Mainz
nodes.note: A Rhine frontier node, known chiefly for the Mainz ritual vessel, whose painted scenes are generally read as an initiation sequence. The figures and actions are visible; their exact liturgical order and meaning remain scholarly reconstruction rather than a preserved instruction.

nodes.name: Böckingen
nodes.note: Preserves altars associated with a centurion of Legio VIII Augusta, one of them dated to 148 CE — among the more securely dated Rhine dedications.

nodes.name: Königshoffen
nodes.note: A sanctuary in the civilian settlement beside the legionary camp of Argentorate, its large relief now held in the Strasbourg museum. It illustrates that a 'military node' commonly meant soldiers, veterans, families, merchants, and service labor together, not the barracks in isolation.

nodes.name: Poetovio
nodes.note: Important for customs administration; evidence here links the cult with personnel of the publicum portorium Illyrici, supporting circulation through imperial fiscal employment alongside troop transfer.

nodes.name: Aquincum
nodes.note: Named among the major Danubian findspots. The dossier's own sources do not detail its building history beyond that classification, which is itself a caution against equating a name on a list with a documented sanctuary.

nodes.name: Sarmizegetusa
nodes.note: Representative of Roman Dacia's abundant Mithraic dedications, which sit oddly against a small number of archaeologically verified buildings — some corpora identify only four excavated mithraea in the whole province, a reminder that inscription density and confirmed sanctuary count are not the same measurement.

nodes.name: London, Walbrook Mithraeum
nodes.note: Built in the third century beside the Walbrook stream. Its small tauroctony was dedicated by Ulpius Silvanus, a veteran of Legio II Augusta, whose formula records only that he fulfilled a vow and installed the image — the route by which he or the image reached London cannot be reconstructed end to end. Discovered in 1954 amid public controversy and hastily relocated, the foundations were more accurately recovered in excavations of 2010–2013; the sanctuary was later rededicated, perhaps to Bacchus, arguing for transformation rather than one abrupt closure.

nodes.name: Carrawburgh
nodes.note: A sanctuary outside the fort of Brocolitia, in a vicus landscape near a spring and the shrine of Coventina. Discovered in 1949 and excavated in 1950, it preserved waterlogged timber through five building phases; its altars name military dedicants alongside local divine powers, a shared ritual landscape rather than an isolated soldiers' chapel. The exposed remains today include modern replicas; the original altars and statues are in museum custody.

nodes.name: Rudchester
nodes.note: A sanctuary outside the fort of Vindobala, producing five altars and sculpture after its discovery in 1844. Pottery suggests the room fell out of use by about the mid-fourth century; nothing in the record explains why.

nodes.name: Housesteads
nodes.note: Named alongside London, Carrawburgh, and Rudchester as a securely attested Wall site. The dossier records no further architectural or epigraphic detail here beyond that identification, which is worth stating plainly rather than padded over.

nodes.name: Sarrebourg
nodes.note: A chained skeleton found here has sometimes been presented as a murdered Mithraic priest buried in a deliberately destroyed sanctuary. The link between the burial, a violent death, a Mithraic identity, and specific perpetrators is not securely established, and the site should not be treated as a solved case of Christian atrocity. Coins once cited as evidence of fifth-century survival here do not establish continued institutional practice.

nodes.name: Angers
nodes.note: Ancient Juliomagus, showing urban adoption of the cult in a town without a legionary fortress — a check against reducing the network to a soldiers' affair.

nodes.name: Tienen
nodes.note: Produced an exceptional ritual deposit — extensive pottery, animal bone, nearly a hundred incense burners, and specially commissioned vessels — interpreted as an outdoor communal banquet far larger than the sanctuary's own room could hold, which complicates any single capacity estimate for the network's meals.

nodes.name: Dura-Europos
nodes.note: The strongest documented case of a specific military unit transplanting and localizing the cult: a sanctuary in block J5, sponsored about 168–171 by soldiers of a Palmyrene archer detachment in Roman service, its dedications in Palmyrene Aramaic and Greek. Enlarged and redecorated across later phases, it ended with the settlement's destruction or abandonment after the Sasanian siege of 256. Where the soldiers were initiated, who taught the ritual, and whether any object physically traveled from Palmyra are not recoverable.

nodes.name: Lambaesis
nodes.note: A legionary base, and the most important North African node in a thinner and more unevenly documented regional record. One inventory counts fifteen Mithraic inscriptions in Numidia against five in Mauretania Caesariensis, two in Mauretania Tingitana, and one at Sabratha — figures that shift with corpus rules and new finds.

nodes.name: C. Sacidius Barbarus
nodes.note: Centurion of Legio XV Apollinaris, and the author of an early military dedication at Carnuntum, dated mainly by inference from his legion's departure for the East under Trajan rather than by a fixed year on the stone itself.

nodes.name: Ethpeni
nodes.note: A Palmyrene military officer or sponsor named in the inscriptions that established the Dura-Europos sanctuary, about 168–171 CE.

nodes.name: Zenobios/Eiaebas
nodes.note: Commander or strategos of the Palmyrene archers, son of Yarhibol, who dedicated at Dura in 170–171.

nodes.name: Palmyrene archer detachment
nodes.note: Palmyrene archers in Roman service, posted to the Euphrates garrison at Dura — the clearest documented instance of a specific unit carrying and localizing the cult. Its dedications name the sponsors Ethpeni and Zenobios/Eiaebas; the unit's cell ended when Dura fell in 256.

nodes.name: Ulpius Silvanus
nodes.note: Veteran of Legio II Augusta who dedicated the small tauroctony at London's Walbrook sanctuary; his formula records fulfillment of a vow, not the route by which he or the image reached the city.

nodes.name: Felicissimus
nodes.note: Donor whose name is attached to one of Ostia's Mithraic sanctuaries, established in the second half of the third century. Nothing beyond the dedication itself is known of him.

nodes.name: Kriton the Athenian
nodes.note: Sculptor, or a sculptor's signing name, on the marble tauroctony of Ostia's Baths of Mithras sanctuary — one of the network's rare named artisans, though whether every surviving 'Criton' reference identifies the same man is debated.

nodes.name: Vettius Agorius Praetextatus
nodes.note: A senator holding numerous pagan priesthoods, described after his death in 384 as pater patrum. His accumulation of titles is evidence of elite participation, not of central control over ordinary cells; nothing shows him directing sanctuaries beyond his own circle.

nodes.name: The Tetrarchs
nodes.note: In 308 the Tetrarchic emperors restored a sanctuary of Mithras at Carnuntum and called him fautor imperii sui, 'supporter of their empire.' The inscription securely documents imperial sponsorship of one major site; what it meant politically is debated, and it does not establish an imperial Mithraic church.

nodes.name: The Roman military-supply corridor
nodes.note: Not an institution of the cult but the pre-existing Roman transport and supply environment — army suppliers, transport contractors, customs staff, merchants, and veteran households — that a 2021 network analysis found correlated with Mithraic site distribution: no statistically significant empire-wide match to fortress locations alone, but a real association with sites on routes joining military centers. The cult rode this infrastructure; it did not own it, and no ancient source describes it as the cult's own system.

edges.note: One converted sanctuary among the city's largely unrecovered concentration of cells.

Linked by the Tiber, the Via Ostiensis, port administration, and labor migration; shared iconography and dense populations make contact probable, but no surviving letter or record proves a formal relationship, scheduled visitation, or transfer of dues between their cells.

Officer careers and unit deployments connected the Danube and Rhine military systems in general; no document traces a specific transfer of cult practice or personnel between these two sites in particular.
Both Rhine frontier dedications; whether either community had any contact with the other is not recorded.
Upper Rhine sites within the same legionary system; proximity does not by itself establish a documented link between the two cells.

The dossier's own caution applies directly here: Legio II Augusta served in Britain and Legio VIII Augusta linked the upper Rhine to wider deployments, but a matching divine image at two bases is not by itself proof that a soldier carried it between them.
Both part of the Danube-Pannonian system; the connection is inferred from shared regional infrastructure, not from a document naming both sites together.
The Danube-to-Dacia chain implied by shared imperial administration; Dacia's abundant dedications against its few excavated buildings warn against reading this as a settled fact.
Neighboring sanctuaries on Hadrian's Wall; a shared frontier corridor is certain, a specific connection between the two congregations is not.
Britain's best-documented sites; whatever connected the province's cells is inferred from shared military and administrative geography, not from any surviving correspondence.

Posted to the Euphrates garrison about 168–171, the detachment founded and sponsored the sanctuary in block J5, translating its vocabulary into Palmyrene Aramaic and Greek rather than importing an unchanged Iranian original. This is the dossier's closest approximation to an end-to-end transfer; even here, who taught the ritual and whether any object traveled from Palmyra are unknown.
The 308 restoration and its fautor imperii sui formula: imperial patronage of one site, not evidence of an imperial Mithraic church.
The 2021 network analysis's own finding: sites disproportionately positioned on transport routes joining military centers, not a significant empire-wide match to fortresses alone.
